overview: This is the atlas’s broad label for several southern Indian states in 1700-1783, especially around Madurai, Thanjavur and Ramnad. It is not one Hindu empire. The 1700 outline also reaches Mysore and the far southwest; the 1715 outline contracts eastward. Neither boundary tracks every changing ruler. This card follows distinct southern courts, their subjects and their dealings with Mughal, Carnatic and European powers.

periods.title: Southern courts and competing claims
periods.summary: Madurai Nayak, Thanjavur Maratha and Ramnad authorities pursued separate interests. Queen Mangammal’s regency belongs to the opening years.

periods.title: Conquest and continued regional courts
periods.summary: Madurai’s Nayak kingdom ended in 1736. Thanjavur continued under Maratha rulers amid Carnatic and European intervention; the atlas retains its broad label.

periods.title: Later transitions beyond the map cutoff
periods.summary: Thanjavur’s administration passed to the British in 1799. A reduced royal establishment survived until annexation in 1855.

sections.title: Several courts, several kinds of power

items.text: Thanjavur’s Maratha kingdom began under Ekoji in the 1670s. Its rulers later paid tribute within the Mughal governor’s southern political order and clashed with Arcot’s nawab. Their southern court should not simply be treated as another name for the whole Maratha Empire.

Madurai’s Queen Mangammal governed as regent for her young grandson. She accepted Mughal tribute demands while negotiating with neighboring powers. The university history records her 1701 land gift to a Muslim dargah. The map’s religious label can hide the practical alliances and varied religious communities of these kingdoms.

A Tamil copper grant dated 1733 names two villages, Suriyan Kuttam and Sembikuttam, and their recipient Anand Iyengar, son of Narayana Iyengar. The grantor’s connection to the Ramnad royal family is also spelled out. Government survives here as named land, named families and a durable legal record.

Ramnad’s Ramalinga Vilasam palace contained both an audience hall and royal living quarters. Built during Kizhavan Sethupathi’s reign, 1674-1710, it brought political ceremony and an elite household into the same complex. Its surviving rooms show a ruler’s residence, not the typical size or comfort of ordinary homes.

sections.title: Roads, shopping and pictures on the walls

items.text: Mangammal’s public works included improved roads toward Rameswaram, tree planting and irrigation. These could matter to travelers and farming households as much as palaces did. The same regional history records severe droughts in 1710 and 1720, a reminder that a ruler’s building projects did not remove dependence on rain.

A 1760 copper plate from Tiruchendur records traders’ monthly expenses for cotton, tobacco and trousers, alongside support for worship at a monastery. The merchants came from several named places, including Sivakasi. Trousers have made it into the historical record: accounting could preserve details that a royal battle story would leave out.

The same plate places this support in Avani, a month of the Tamil calendar, and decorates the record with Murugan and his consorts, Ganesha and a peacock. Religious gatherings, merchant contributions and crafted legal documents intersected. Its copper sheet is roughly 37 centimeters tall, a fairly substantial receipt to put in your pocket.

Ramnad’s palace paintings depict battles with Thanjavur’s Marathas and contacts with Europeans. They also include Ramayana scenes and water sports, with descriptions in colloquial language. Walls could present stories as well as royal prestige. These are courtly representations; a painted activity does not prove that every household enjoyed it.

A copper coin catalogued as an eighteenth-century Madurai Nayak issue weighs 2.1 grams and measures only 1.2 centimeters across. Its reverse gives the Tamil city name Madurai in two lines. The museum does not know where this particular coin was found or assign it to a named king, so its date remains broad.

The Saraswathi Mahal Library grew from a Nayak court collection and received support from Thanjavur’s Maratha rulers. Manuscripts made earlier scholarship available to later readers. The especially famous collecting of Serfoji II belongs mainly after 1798, beyond this map interval; it should not be quietly moved back into 1700.

Tulaja I, also called Tukkoji, was a royal author whose medical works survive in the Thanjavur manuscript tradition. Scholar V. Raghavan identified Dhanvantarivilasa as a work written at the request of Tulaja’s son Ekoji. This is a concrete family connection in the production of learned medicine.

Raghavan also described a compilation attributed to Tulaja containing medical formulas and lists of Sanskrit herb names with Tamil equivalents. Naming a plant in more than one language helped connect kinds of learned knowledge. These learned compilations do not tell us how widely treatment was available.

Shahaji’s early eighteenth-century Telugu opera Pallaki Seva Prabandha draws on ritual at Tiruvarur. Parvati’s companions try to approach Shiva, who eventually travels to her in a palanquin. Songs, spoken narrative links and verse carry the story. The imagined divine court even makes room for the poet-king’s own work.

A short Telugu sample, in the Music Academy’s modern Roman transliteration, is kadalimpakurōyi pallaki: “Don’t swing the pallaki so.” A pallaki is a palanquin. In the song’s playful religious imagery, careful bearers must avoid disturbing the worlds within the god. This presents a transmitted period text, not the handwriting of Shahaji.

The opera survived through both manuscripts and performers. In the twentieth century P. Sambhamoorthy located its songs in the singing of Veerammal and wrote down their music. His 1955 edition printed Telugu lyrics and Tamil-script notation. Spoken language and the script used to record music need not be the same thing.

ending.text: No single kingdom fell in 1783. Madurai’s Nayak rule ended with Chanda Sahib’s conquest in 1736, while Thanjavur’s Maratha court continued. Thanjavur transferred administration to the British in 1799 and retained a smaller royal establishment until 1855. The atlas cutoff is not the disappearance of southern communities, their languages or their cultural traditions.
